title: Compact QBR metric definitions and KPI matrix
summary: Short, operational definitions for the four core QBR metrics (latency, uptime, cost/token, cache hit rate) plus a compact KPI matrix and quick extraction checklist for QBR preparation.
body:
Purpose:
This is a compact reference for Customer Success managers preparing QBRs. It standardizes how we define, compute, and flag the four metrics that matter most to customers running production inference on Redwood: latency, uptime, cost per token, and cache hit rate. Use this doc as a checklist and a copy-paste source for queries and slides.

Audience:
CS leads, renewal owners, solutions engineers, and SRE partners who provide metric evidence in quarterly business reviews.

Data sources and instrumentation notes (high level):
- Primary sources: BigQuery event logs (ingest: token-level traces, request metadata), Prometheus for infra-level uptime and CPU/GPU availability, billing export for cost aggregation, and Redis/serving-runtime internal metrics for cache hits.
- Important join keys: customer_id, deployment_id, model_name, timestamp, request_id.
- Timezones: normalize all timestamps to UTC for QBR aggregates.

Metric definitions and how to compute them (operational):
1) Latency (response generation time)
   - Definition: end-to-end server-side latency per request measured from the time the request reaches the inference front end to the time the final token is emitted (server-side). Excludes client network time.
   - Key percentiles: P50 (median), P95, P99. Report both overall and broken out by model and route.
   - Formula (per window):
       collect lat_ms for each request -> compute percentiles over window
   - Typical query notes: filter out cold-starts (first N requests after a process restart) and very large sequence-length outliers (>99.9th percentile) unless the customer specifically uses long-context workloads.

2) Uptime (service availability)
   - Definition: fraction of time the serving endpoint satisfies health checks and returns 2xx for production route traffic (weighted by requests). We compute both availability by route and by control-plane (management API) separately.
   - Measurement window: rolling 30d SLA and QBR quarter-to-date.
   - Formula examples:
       uptime = 1 - (sum(request_failures_due_to_service_unavailable) / total_production_requests)
       or via health pings: uptime = successful_pings / total_pings
   - Important: distinguish between transient client errors (4xx) and server-side availability issues (5xx, timeouts, connection failures). Only count server-side unavailability against uptime SLA.

3) Cost per token (unit economics)
   - Definition: total serving cost allocated to the customer divided by the number of tokens generated+consumed (inbound + outbound tokens) in the window. We present both grossed cost and unit cost after applied credits/commits.
   - Cost components to include: GPU runtime (by instance type), inference licensing (if any), quantization/CPU fallback costs, and network egress where billable. Do not include sales credits or offsetting discounts in the raw cost view; those are shown separately in the billing summary.
   - Formula (simplified):
       cost_per_token = sum(cost_components_for_window) / sum(tokens_in + tokens_out)
   - Notes: report both median and 95th percentile of per-request token counts to show distribution; a few large generating requests can skew average cost-per-token.

4) Cache hit rate (prefix/KV cache effectiveness)
   - Definition: percentage of requests where a cache (prefix cache or KV cache for decoder state) meaningfully reduced compute (i.e., avoided recomputing prefix tokens or reusing KV entries).
   - Measurement: compute hits and misses from serving-runtime counters (cache_hits, cache_lookups) and also track estimated compute-savings (token-equivalent savings).
   - Formula:
       cache_hit_rate = sum(cache_hits) / sum(cache_lookups)
       effective_token_savings = sum(estimated_tokens_saved_by_cache)
   - Operational nuance: report separate values for prefix cache vs KV cache and by model family. Some model architectures see much higher prefix reuse.

Compact KPI matrix (copy into QBR slide table)
Columns: Metric | Definition (one line) | QBR Target | Measurement window | Owner | Action trigger
Rows:
- Latency | Server-side P95 response time | P95 < 250 ms (hosted small models), see customer SLA | Quarterly (and 30d rolling) | CS + SRE | P95 increased > 30% quarter-over-quarter or absolute breach vs SLA
- Uptime | Production route availability | 99.9% monthly (SLA) | Monthly + QTD | CS + SRE | Any month < SLA or >2 incidents causing >5min outage each
- Cost / token | Serving cost divided by tokens | Customer-dependent; show baseline + +/- 15% target | Quarterly | CS + Solutions Eng | Cost per token up >20% QoQ or unusual spike without traffic pattern change
- Cache hit rate | Prefix/KV cache hit % | > 40% (depending on workload) | 30d rolling | Solutions Eng + Runtime Eng | Hit rate falls >10pp or savings drop >20%

Quick extraction checklist for a QBR run (data workstream):
- Confirm quarter dates and timezone normalization.
- Run latency percentiles query (P50/P95/P99) by model and route.
- Extract the uptime summary: total requests, server-side failures, health ping success ratio.
- Generate cost allocation: map billing export to deployment ids, aggregate cost components for the quarter, divide by token counts.
- Pull cache metrics: cache_lookups, cache_hits, estimated token savings; break out by model and route.
- Create a one-slide KPI table and one slide with trend charts (30d, 90d, QoQ).
- For any metric in action-trigger state, collect incident timelines, remediation steps, and next-steps slide.

Sample BigQuery snippets (pseudocode, adapt to repo queries):
- latency percentiles: SELECT quantiles(lat_ms, [0.5,0.95,0.99]) FROM `events` WHERE customer_id = @cust AND ts BETWEEN @start AND @end ;
- uptime: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status_code >=500 OR status = 'timeout' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) as failure_rate FROM `requests` WHERE customer_id=@cust AND ts BETWEEN @start AND @end ;
- cache hit rate: SELECT SUM(cache_hits) / SUM(cache_lookups) as hit_rate FROM `serving_cache` WHERE customer_id=@cust AND ts BETWEEN @start AND @end ;

Presentation tips and talking points:
- For latency: show both percentiles and distribution (histogram). Call out traffic shifts (longer prompts, more function calls) that explain changes.
- For cost: normalize cost per 1M tokens to make comparisons easier. Show model mix (percent of traffic by model) since model upgrades/rollouts can change unit economics.
- For cache: convert savings to dollars for business impact (estimated tokens saved * cost_per_token).

Open questions / TODOs for CS owners:
- Agree on customer-specific latency targets (hosted vs dedicated vs private) and record them in the renewal tracker.
- Confirm whether to include managed-control-plane downtime in uptime for each customer SLA.
- Standardize the list of model families for breakouts (gpt-like, llama-like, encoder-only for embeddings).

Appendix: common flags and definitions (one line each):
- Cold-start: first request after process/container restart that misses warmed caches and creates inflated latency; exclude for steady-state metrics unless customer cares.
- Request-weighted uptime: availability measured weighted by actual requests rather than simple ping counts.
- Token accounting: inbound prompt tokens + model-generated tokens (include function-call tokens if applicable).

Maintainer note: copy this doc into the customer-specific QBR folder, update the KPI target row values to match that customer’s contract and expected model mix before presenting.

End of doc.
